title: What do translators charge per word and how to calculate your own rate

description: Learn what do translators charge per word and why guessing your rate hurts your business. Use this guide to calculate a sustainable rate on your Mac.

intro: Translators typically charge between 0.08 and 0.25 USD per word, depending on language pair, subject matter, and experience. However, asking what do translators charge per word is often the wrong starting point for your business.
tldr: Stop guessing your rates based on industry averages that do not account for your specific costs.
Calculate your bottom-up rate using your target annual revenue divided by your total billable capacity.
Track your actual output for one week to stop overestimating your daily word count.
Use software like Harvest to track non-billable admin time that eats into your profit.
Diversify your client base between agencies and direct clients to balance volume and higher margins.

blocks.text: The agency trap and why market rates are misleading

Many translators start by asking what do translators charge per word on public forums. They then adopt the lowest common denominator. This is the agency trap. You accept rates that cover the agency overhead but ignore your own business costs. You pay for your own Mac, your own software, your own insurance, and your own taxes. If your rate does not factor these in, you are subsidizing your client.
How to calculate your minimum viable rate

You must use a bottom-up formula. Start with your target annual revenue. Subtract your business expenses. Divide the remainder by the number of days you can realistically work. Then divide by your true daily word output. If you aim for 60,000 USD and work 200 days a year, you need 300 USD per day. If you can only translate 2,000 words a day comfortably, your minimum rate is 0.15 USD per word. Anything less is a loss.

items: Annual revenue target: The total amount you need to earn.
Business expenses: Software, hardware, insurance, and professional memberships.
Productive days: Be honest. You cannot bill 365 days a year.
Average daily word output: Measure this over a full week, not just your best day.

blocks.text: Hidden costs that erode your profit

Translators often forget the time spent on non-billable tasks. You spend hours on invoicing, tax preparation, and file management. These are not billable hours. You must include this time in your calculation. If you spend 20 percent of your time on admin, your effective hourly rate drops by 20 percent. You must charge enough to cover that lost time.
Fixes anyone can use without buying anything

First, track your time for one week. Use the Clock app on your Mac. Note when you start a project and when you finish. Record the number of words delivered. You will likely find your output is lower than you think. Second, audit your expenses. Cancel unused subscriptions. Third, stop accepting MTPE rates that are too low. If the effort is 80 percent of a full translation, the rate should be at least 70 percent of your standard rate.
If you handle medical or legal documents, follow your client's exact instructions for data security. Never use public AI tools to process sensitive or private client data.

faq.question: What do translators charge per word for beginners?
faq.answer: Beginners often start lower, but you should still calculate your floor. Aim to reach a sustainable rate as soon as you gain experience.

faq.question: How do I account for CAT tool discounts?
faq.answer: Only offer discounts for exact matches. Use the analysis function in your CAT tool to show the client exactly why the price is lower.

faq.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the word?
faq.answer: Per word is the industry standard. However, you should know your hourly equivalent to ensure you are meeting your financial targets.

costs.title: Financial instability
costs.text: Charging too little means you must work longer hours just to pay basic bills.

costs.title: Burnout
costs.text: The pressure to take on high volumes of low-paying work leads to exhaustion and mental fatigue.

costs.title: Reduced quality
costs.text: Rushed work increases the risk of errors, which can be catastrophic in specialized fields.

causes.title: Ignoring overhead
causes.text: Many translators treat their revenue as profit, forgetting to subtract software, hardware, and tax costs.

causes.title: Overestimating output
causes.text: Translators often base their rates on their best days rather than their sustainable daily average.

causes.title: Accepting agency rates
causes.text: Inheriting rates from agencies without performing your own cost analysis creates a cycle of undercharging.

fixes.title: Use a bottom-up formula
fixes.text: Calculate your rate based on your target income and true productive capacity.

fixes.title: Track your time
fixes.text: Measure your actual output for one week to establish a realistic baseline for your pricing.

fixes.title: Diversify your client base
fixes.text: Balance lower-paying agency work with higher-paying direct clients to protect your bottom line.
